mekki-muskil:1-1.t:
His saying, the Exalted: (إذا زلزلت): (إذا) is an adverb of future time, and the governor in it is (زلزلت). That is permissible because it carries the meaning of a condition, and what follows it is, in the implied structure, jussive through it. Just as it is permissible for it to govern what follows it while in rule it is annexed to the clause after it, so it is permissible for what follows it to govern it, as with (من) and (ما) that are conditional: what follows them governs them, and they govern what follows them. You say (من تكرم أكرمه) and (ما تفعل أفعل); (ما) and (من) are in the position of the accusative by the jussive verb after them, and they made jussive what follows them. So (إذا), since it carries the meaning of a condition, went the way of (ما) and (من), even though in the implied structure it is annexed to the clause after it. [Translator's note: the source has a stray letter «ة» in «بعدهما ة تعملان», probably a wāw.]
His saying (زلزالها): a maṣdar (verbal noun), as you say (ضربتك ضربك). Its annexation to the pronoun is good so that the verse endings agree in one form. (الزلزال) with fatḥa is the noun and with kasra the maṣdar; it is also said that both are maṣdars. ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read (وزلزلوا زلزالا) with fatḥa, and read (زلزالها) with fatḥa.

mekki-muskil:3-3.t: His saying (ما لها): (ما) is a mubtadaʾ (subject); it is interrogative, a complete noun (ism tāmm), and (لها) is the khabar (predicate).

mekki-muskil:7-7.t: His saying (فمن يعمل مثقال): (من) is conditional; it is a complete noun (ism tāmm) and a mubtadaʾ (subject), and (يره) is the khabar (predicate). The second one is like it.
